solution:
A **bidentate ligand** is a polydentate ligand that has **two donor atoms**, both of which link to the same central metal ion.

The chapter gives two examples:

**Ethylenediamine (en)** — it binds to the metal using the lone pair on each of its two nitrogen atoms, \(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\).

**Oxalate ion**, \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2\ominus}}\) — it uses the electron pair on each of its two negatively charged oxygen atoms.

Because each such ligand supplies two donor atoms, it contributes 2 to the coordination number of the metal, not 1.

**Coordination number.** All six ligands inside the square bracket — one \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) and five \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) — are monodentate, so each supplies one donor atom.

\(\mathrm{C.N.} = 1 + 5 = 6\)

**Oxidation state.** The charge on the complex ion is \(-1\). Ammonia is neutral and each chloride is \(-1\), so

\(x + 1(0) + 5(-1) = -1\), giving \(x = +4\).

The coordination number of platinum is **6** and its oxidation state is **\(+4\)**. A coordination number of six means the complex is octahedral.

Both are formed by combining two or more stable compounds in a stoichiometric ratio, but they behave differently in water.

**Double salt :** it dissociates in water **completely into simple ions**. Example — Mohr's salt, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4(NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O}\) :

\(\mathrm{FeSO_4(NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{water}} \mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)}\)

**Coordination complex :** it dissociates in water to give **at least one complex ion**, which stays intact in solution. Example — \(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}\) :

\(\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{K^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}(aq)}\)

Here \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) is the counter ion while \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4\ominus}}\) is the complex ion; the solution gives no test for free \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\) or free \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\).

The test is the chapter's: a complex in which the metal ion is bound to only ONE type of ligand is **homoleptic**; one in which it is surrounded by MORE THAN ONE type of ligand is **heteroleptic**. Only what is inside the coordination sphere counts.

**\(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]SO_4}\) — homoleptic.** The sphere \(\mathrm{[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2\oplus}}\) holds four ammine ligands and nothing else; \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) is only the counter ion.

**\(\mathrm{[Cu(en)_2(H_2O)Cl]^{2\oplus}}\) — heteroleptic.** Three different ligands: ethylenediamine, aqua and chloro.

**\(\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_5(NCS)]^{2\oplus}}\) — heteroleptic.** Two different ligands: aqua and isothiocyanato.

**Tetraammine zinc (II) nitrate, \(\mathrm{[Zn(NH_3)_4](NO_3)_2}\) — homoleptic.** The sphere holds four ammine ligands only; the two nitrate ions lie outside it.

**a. Potassium amminetrichloroplatinate (II)**

'Platinate' shows the complex ion is anionic and '(II)' fixes platinum at \(+2\). The ligands are one ammine and three chloro, so

charge \(= +2 + 1(0) + 3(-1) = -1\)

One potassium ion balances it.

**Formula :** \(\mathrm{K[Pt(NH_3)Cl_3]}\)

**b. Dicyanoaurate (I) ion**

'Aurate' is the name of gold in an anionic complex and '(I)' fixes gold at \(+1\); 'dicyano' means two \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\) ligands.

charge \(= +1 + 2(-1) = -1\)

**Formula :** \(\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^{\ominus}}\)

(This is the very ion the chapter mentions in \(\mathrm{K[Au(CN)_2]}\), used in the electroplating of gold.)

**Ionization isomers** are structural isomers that involve the **exchange of ligands between the coordination sphere and the ionization sphere**. They have the same molecular formula but give different ions in solution.

**Example**, from the chapter :

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}\)

In the first, the sulphate is bonded to cobalt inside the coordination sphere and bromide is the counter ion; in the second they have swapped places. On dissolution they ionise differently:

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\)

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]^{2\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\)

so the two can be told apart by the ions each releases.

The distinction comes from the size of the crystal field splitting parameter \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) compared with the energy needed to pair two electrons in the same orbital.

**Low-spin complexes** are formed with **strong field ligands**. Here \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) is large, so it costs less energy to pair electrons in the lower \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) set than to promote one to the upper \(\mathrm{e_g}\) set. Pairing is favoured, and the complex has the SMALLEST possible number of unpaired electrons. Example — \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3\oplus}}\), whose electrons are all paired.

**High-spin complexes** are formed with **weak field ligands**. Here \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) is smaller than the electron pairing energy, so the electrons occupy both sets singly before any pairing occurs, and the complex has the LARGEST possible number of unpaired electrons. Example — \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3\ominus}}\), which has four unpaired electrons.

The chapter notes that the two are distinguishable only for the \(\mathrm{d^4}\) to \(\mathrm{d^7}\) configurations; for \(\mathrm{d^1}\), \(\mathrm{d^2}\), \(\mathrm{d^3}\), \(\mathrm{d^8}\), \(\mathrm{d^9}\) and \(\mathrm{d^{10}}\) the two arrangements are the same.

**Oxidation state.** \(x + 4(-1) = -2\), so cobalt is \(\mathrm{Co^{2\oplus}}\).

**Free metal ion.** Cobalt is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^7 4s^2}\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{2\oplus}}\) is \(\mathrm{3d^7}\). Writing each orbital as a box, and \(\uparrow\downarrow\) for a pair and \(\uparrow\) for a single electron:

**\(\mathrm{Co^{2\oplus}}\) (free ion)**

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\ )\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\ )(\ )(\ )\)

**After complex formation.** Four chloride ligands need four vacant metal orbitals. The complex is tetrahedral, so the \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons are NOT disturbed and the four orbitals are taken from the next shell:

\(\mathrm{3d} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4s} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)\)   \(\mathrm{4p} :\) \((\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)(\uparrow\downarrow)\)

where the four pairs shown in \(\mathrm{4s}\) and \(\mathrm{4p}\) are the electron pairs donated by the four \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) ligands.

**Orbitals participating in hybridisation :** one \(\mathrm{4s}\) orbital and three \(\mathrm{4p}\) orbitals, giving **\(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridisation** — which is what makes the complex tetrahedral.

Three \(\mathrm{3d}\) electrons remain unpaired, so the complex is paramagnetic.

The chapter classifies ligands by how large a crystal field splitting \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) they produce.

**Strong field ligands** are those in which the donor atoms are **C, N or P**. They approach the metal closely, cause a large splitting of the d orbitals, favour pairing of electrons and so tend to form low-spin complexes. **Example :** the cyanide ion \(\mathrm{CN^{\ominus}}\) (others listed are \(\mathrm{NC^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{CO}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), EDTA and en).

**Weak field ligands** are those in which the donor atoms are **halogens, oxygen or sulphur**. For these \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) is smaller than the electron pairing energy, so pairing is not favoured. **Example :** the fluoride ion \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\) (others listed are \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{I^{\ominus}}\), \(\mathrm{SCN^{\ominus}}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2\ominus}}\)).

The chapter's spectrochemical series arranges them in order of increasing field strength :

\(\mathrm{I^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{Br^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{S^{2\ominus}} < \mathrm{F^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2\ominus}} < \mathrm{H_2O} < \mathrm{NCS^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{EDTA} < \mathrm{NH_3} < \mathrm{en} < \mathrm{CN^{\ominus}} < \mathrm{CO}\)

**Oxidation state and d count.** Ethylenediamine is neutral, so \(x + 3(0) = +3\) gives \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\). Chromium is \(\mathrm{[Ar]3d^5 4s^1}\), so \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\) is a \(\mathrm{d^3}\) ion.

**Crystal field energy-level diagram.** Six ligands approach along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes, and the five degenerate d orbitals split into two sets separated by \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) :

upper set \(\mathrm{e_g}\) — \((\mathrm{d_{x^2-y^2}},\ \mathrm{d_{z^2}})\), raised by \(0.6\,\Delta_\mathrm{o}\)

lower set \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) — \((\mathrm{d_{xy}},\ \mathrm{d_{yz}},\ \mathrm{d_{zx}})\), lowered by \(0.4\,\Delta_\mathrm{o}\)

The three d electrons occupy the three \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) orbitals singly, obeying Hund's rule, and the \(\mathrm{e_g}\) set is empty :

\(\mathrm{e_g} :\) \((\ )(\ )\)

\(\mathrm{t_{2g}} :\) \((\uparrow)(\uparrow)(\uparrow)\)

**Why it is coloured.** Because the \(\mathrm{e_g}\) set is vacant, an electron can be promoted from \(\mathrm{t_{2g}}\) to \(\mathrm{e_g}\) — a **d-d transition**. The energy needed is exactly \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\), which for this complex corresponds to a frequency of electromagnetic radiation in the VISIBLE region. The complex absorbs that wavelength from white light, and the colour we see is the colour complementary to the one absorbed. This is the same mechanism the chapter uses to explain the violet colour of \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3\oplus}}\).

(Note that en is a strong field ligand, so \(\Delta_\mathrm{o}\) here is relatively large.)
